How this book matches your board exam. Research check: this book follows NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 1 (Chemical Reactions and Equations), for the CBSE 2026–27 session. The Science theory paper is 80 marks in 3 hours, plus 20 marks of internal assessment. The question paper design is the same as 2025–26, and the two board exams continue: Phase 1 is compulsory, and Phase 2 is optional for improving marks. Questions range from 1-mark MCQs and assertion–reason items to 2-, 3- and 5-mark answers and 4-mark case-based questions, and about half the paper tests competency (applying ideas to new situations).

Each unit ends with a 10-mark practice set built from these question types. Every chemical equation in this book has been checked to be balanced. The marking points are our own, written for practice, not the official CBSE marking scheme. Check the latest sample paper on cbseacademic.nic.in before your exam.

Unit 1 of 10: Recognising a Chemical Reaction

Key ideas

  • In a chemical change, new substances with new properties form. In a physical change, no new substance forms (for example melting ice or dissolving sugar).
  • Signs of a chemical reaction: a change in state, a change in colour, the evolution of a gas, a change in temperature, or the formation of a precipitate (an insoluble solid).
  • Many reactions show more than one sign. Not every sign proves a reaction on its own: boiling water releases a gas (steam), but it is a physical change.

Worked examples

Example 1: burning magnesium ribbon (NCERT Activity 1.1). Clean the ribbon with sandpaper first to remove the oxide layer. It burns with a dazzling white flame and forms a white powder, magnesium oxide: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Signs: light, heat, and a new white solid.

Example 2: lead nitrate and potassium iodide. Mixing the two colourless solutions forms a yellow precipitate of lead iodide. Signs: colour change and a precipitate.

Example 3: zinc and dilute sulphuric acid. Bubbles of hydrogen gas form and the flask becomes warm: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Signs: a gas and a temperature change.

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) Which is a chemical change? (a) melting wax (b) dissolving salt (c) souring of milk (d) boiling water. Answer: (c).
  2. (1 mark, assertion–reason) Assertion (A): magnesium ribbon is cleaned before burning. Reason (R): magnesium reacts with oxygen in air to form a layer of magnesium oxide. (a) Both true and R explains A (b) Both true but R does not explain A (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true. Answer: (a).
  3. (2 marks) List four observations that show a chemical reaction has taken place. Answer: change in state, change in colour, evolution of a gas, change in temperature (or a precipitate). Half a mark each.
  4. (3 marks) Describe what you observe when zinc granules are added to dilute sulphuric acid, and write the balanced equation. Answer: bubbles of colourless gas (1); the flask feels warm (1); Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ (1).
  5. (3 marks) Why is the burning of magnesium a chemical change while the melting of ice is a physical change? Answer: burning forms a new substance (magnesium oxide) with different properties and cannot be easily reversed (2); melting ice forms no new substance; water can be refrozen (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Calling every gas evolution a chemical change. 2. Forgetting to clean the magnesium ribbon. 3. Writing "white smoke" instead of "white powder (magnesium oxide)". 4. Missing the temperature change as a sign. 5. Confusing a precipitate with a solution.

Quick recall

  1. What is a precipitate? 2. Name the product of burning magnesium. 3. Give two signs of a chemical reaction. 4. Is souring of milk physical or chemical? 5. What gas forms when zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid?

Answers: 1) An insoluble solid formed in a solution. 2) Magnesium oxide. 3) For example colour change and gas evolution. 4) Chemical. 5) Hydrogen.
